scope: Compute average and RMS output voltage, current and power of half-wave and full-wave phase-controlled rectifiers as a function of the firing angle, and rate the thyristors and free-wheeling path for inductive loads.
intuition: A phase-controlled rectifier is an uncontrolled rectifier with a deliberate delay: the thyristor blocks until the AC source has risen to whatever level you choose, so you control the delivered voltage by throwing away the first slice of every half-cycle. Average voltage therefore falls monotonically from the full uncontrolled value at $\alpha=0$ to zero at $\alpha=180^\circ$.
concept: **The firing-angle convention and why the average voltage has that cosine form.** With $v_s=V_m\sin\omega t$ and the SCR gated at $\alpha$, the load sees $v_s$ only from $\omega t=\alpha$ to $\pi$ (half-wave) or to $\pi+\alpha$ (full-wave). The average of a sine over the remaining conduction window is $V_{avg}=\dfrac{V_m}{2\pi}(1+\cos\alpha)$ for one SCR and $V_{avg}=\dfrac{V_m}{\pi}(1+\cos\alpha)$ for a bridge, because the bridge delivers *two* identical pulses per cycle. Both expressions contain the whole design story: at $\alpha=0$ the bracket is 2 and the half-wave value collapses to the familiar uncontrolled $V_m/\pi$ (and the bridge to $2V_m/\pi$), at $\alpha=90^\circ$ it is exactly 1 (half of full output), and at $\alpha=180^\circ$ it is 0. Angles are always in **degrees** on the board; the formula needs $\alpha$ in radians only inside $\sin(2\alpha)$-type RMS expressions, so convert deliberately and never mix.

**RMS is the waveform that sets heating, and it does not fall as fast as the average.** Because the average is over a shortened window, the form factor rises sharply as $\alpha$ increases: the same SCR that gives $V_{avg}=40.5\ \mathrm{V}$ at $\alpha=60^\circ$ has $V_{rms}=81.1\ \mathrm{V}$, a form factor near 2. This is why the load's $I^2R$ heating and the thyristor's own $I_{rms}^2R_{on}$ loss must use the RMS expressions $V_{rms}=V_m\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\left(\pi-\alpha+\dfrac{\sin 2\alpha}{2}\right)}$ for half-wave and $V_m\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{\pi}\left(\pi-\alpha+\dfrac{\sin2\alpha}{2}\right)}$ for the bridge, not the average. At $\alpha=0$ the bridge square root becomes $\sqrt{1}=1$, so $V_{rms}=V_m/\sqrt2=V_{s,rms}$: with no delay the load sees the entire sine, which is a useful sanity check.

**Triggering and commutation.** The SCR is a latching device: a short gate pulse of a few tens of milliamperes (referenced to cathode) fires it, and it then stays on by itself until its anode current falls below the holding current $I_H$. In a line-commutated rectifier that happens naturally at the AC zero crossing, when the source voltage reverses and the current is forced to zero — this is **natural (line) commutation**, and it is why these circuits need no forced turn-off circuitry. The gate pulse must still be present at the right instant and, with an inductive load, must be either a wide pulse or a train of pulses, because the anode current may not have reached the latching current $I_L$ before a narrow pulse ends.

**Inductive loads and the free-wheeling diode.** With a purely resistive load the current falls to zero with the voltage at $\omega t=\pi$ and the SCR turns off. With a large inductance the current cannot stop instantly, so it keeps flowing past $\pi$ (the load voltage goes negative) and the SCR stays on until the current itself reaches zero at the **extinction angle** $\beta>\pi$. That is why $V_{avg}$ for an RL load can be *lower* than the resistive formula, and why it can even go negative in inversion mode. Adding a **free-wheeling diode** across the load gives the inductor current a path that bypasses the source, so the current free-wheels through the diode while the load voltage is clamped to about one diode drop instead of a large negative value: the output never reverses, the average voltage is raised, the extra negative excursion is removed, and the SCR turns off cleanly at $\pi$. Without it, an RL load both reduces the average output and makes the diode's own reverse recovery and the SCR's $dv/dt$ worse.

formulas.n: One SCR, resistive load, alpha in degrees. At alpha = 0 this is the uncontrolled V_m/pi; at 180 deg it is zero.
Two pulses per cycle, exactly twice the half-wave value. At alpha = 0 it is 2 V_m/pi.
alpha inside sin(2 alpha) must be in radians. Use this for load I^2R heating and for SCR loss, never the average.
Bridge. At alpha = 0 the root is 1, so V_rms = V_m/sqrt(2) = the source rms; a quick check that the formula is right.
Resistive load. This, not the average, sets the load power P = I_rms^2 R_L and the SCR conduction loss I_rms^2 R_on; with an RL load replace R_L by the load impedance magnitude.
For a half-wave SCR with a resistive load. It grows without bound as alpha approaches 180 deg, so a meter reading average badly misstates heating.
Half-wave and bridge alike see V_m in the reverse direction (bridge: each of the two conducting devices blocks V_m; the bridge pair PIV is V_m, the centre-tap is 2 V_m).
Half-wave converter with the current smoothed to a constant I_d and no free-wheeling diode. At alpha = 120 deg this is -27.0 V, so the average reverses and the converter inverts.
The free-wheeling diode clamps the load voltage at about 0.7 V so it never reverses, restores the resistive-formula average, and lets the SCR commutate at the zero crossing.

problems.prompt: A half-wave SCR rectifier is fed from $120\ \mathrm{V}$ rms, 60 Hz and drives a $50\ \Omega$ resistor. The SCR is fired at $\alpha=60^\circ$. Find $V_m$, $V_{o,avg}$, $V_{o,rms}$, the average and RMS load current, and the load power.
steps: Peak: $V_m=\sqrt2(120)=169.7\ \mathrm{V}$.

RMS: $\pi-\alpha+\dfrac{\sin2\alpha}{2}$ with $\alpha=1.0472\ \mathrm{rad}$ gives $3.1416-1.0472+\dfrac{\sin120^\circ}{2}=2.0944+0.4330=2.5274$; divide by $2\pi$ to get $0.40225$, take the root: $0.6342$.
Currents: $I_{avg}=40.5/50=0.810\ \mathrm{A}$ and $I_{rms}=107.6/50=2.152\ \mathrm{A}$.
Load power: $P=I_{rms}^2R_L=(2.152)^2(50)=231.6\ \mathrm{W}$, which is much more than $V_{avg}I_{avg}=32.8\ \mathrm{W}$.
problems.trap: Computing the load power as $V_{avg}I_{avg}=32.8\ \mathrm{W}$. The resistor heats on the RMS waveform, so the correct value is $232\ \mathrm{W}$ — a factor of 7 error at $\alpha=60^\circ$, and far worse at larger $\alpha$.

problems.prompt: Repeat for a full-wave bridge controlled rectifier on the same $120\ \mathrm{V}$ rms source, $50\ \Omega$ load, $\alpha=60^\circ$. Find $V_{o,avg}$, $V_{o,rms}$ and the power, and compare with the half-wave results.
steps: Average is double the half-wave case: $V_{o,avg}=\dfrac{169.7}{\pi}(1+\cos60^\circ)=54.02(1.5)=81.0\ \mathrm{V}$.
RMS bracket: divide 2.5274 by $\pi$ instead of $2\pi$ to get $0.80450$; the root is $0.8969$.
Power: $P=(3.044)^2(50)=463.3\ \mathrm{W}$, and each SCR carries $I_{avg}/2=0.810\ \mathrm{A}$ average.
problems.ans: $V_{o,avg}=81.0\ \mathrm{V}$, $V_{o,rms}=152.2\ \mathrm{V}$, $I_{rms}=3.04\ \mathrm{A}$, $P=463\ \mathrm{W}$; the bridge delivers exactly twice the half-wave average voltage at the same firing angle.
problems.trap: Using the half-wave formula for the bridge (getting 40.5 V instead of 81.0 V), or dividing the bridge RMS by $2\pi$ instead of $\pi$. The bridge produces two identical pulses per cycle, so both average and RMS formulas double relative to the single-SCR case.

problems.prompt: For the full-wave bridge above, find the power dissipated in each SCR if its on-state drop is modelled by $R_{on}=0.05\ \Omega$, and check the average device current against its average rating.
steps: Each SCR conducts one half-cycle of the pair pattern; for a bridge with a resistive load the device RMS current is $I_{rms}/\sqrt2=3.044/1.414=2.152\ \mathrm{A}$.
Conduction loss: $P_{SCR}=I_{SCR,rms}^2R_{on}=(2.152)^2(0.05)=0.2316\ \mathrm{W}$ per device.
Average device current: $I_{SCR,avg}=1.620/2=0.810\ \mathrm{A}$.
Total SCR loss in the bridge is $4(0.232)=0.93\ \mathrm{W}$ (or $2\times0.232$ if two devices share each conduction path), negligible next to the $463\ \mathrm{W}$ load.
problems.ans: About $0.232\ \mathrm{W}$ per SCR, $0.810\ \mathrm{A}$ average per device — the losses are small, but they set the heatsink requirement and the loss scales with $I_{rms}^2$, not with the average.
problems.trap: Using the load average current $1.62\ \mathrm{A}$ in $I^2R$ to get $0.131\ \mathrm{W}$, or forgetting that PWM/phase-controlled RMS currents are much larger than average. The loss is 76 percent too low in this case, and the error grows as $\alpha$ increases.

problems.prompt: A half-wave SCR with a *very large* inductance (so the current is essentially constant, $I_d$) and negligible resistance is fired at $\alpha=120^\circ$. Explain why the extinction angle is no longer $180^\circ$, then find $V_{o,avg}$ for $V_m=169.7\ \mathrm{V}$. What does the free-wheeling diode change?
give: L very large, R negligible (I_d constant)
steps: First apply the resistive formula as a reference: $V_{o,avg}=\dfrac{169.7}{2\pi}(1+\cos120^\circ)=\dfrac{169.7}{6.283}(1-0.5)=27.01(0.5)=13.5\ \mathrm{V}$.

That value assumes the SCR stops conducting at $\omega t=\pi$. With a large inductance the current cannot stop there, so the SCR stays on through a negative half-cycle of source voltage until the current itself reaches zero: the extinction angle is $\beta=\pi+\alpha$, and the load voltage is negative from $\pi$ to $\pi+\alpha$.

Re-integrate over the real window: $V_{o,avg}=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\displaystyle\int_{\alpha}^{\pi+\alpha}V_m\sin\omega t\,d(\omega t)=\dfrac{V_m}{2\pi}\left[-\cos\omega t\right]_{\alpha}^{\pi+\alpha}=\dfrac{V_m}{2\pi}(\cos\alpha+\cos\alpha)=\dfrac{V_m\cos\alpha}{\pi}$.

Numerically $V_{o,avg}=\dfrac{169.7\cos120^\circ}{\pi}=\dfrac{-84.85}{\pi}=-27.0\ \mathrm{V}$: with the current still positive the converter delivers *negative* average voltage, which is inversion (power flowing from the DC side back to the AC source).

Adding the free-wheeling diode clamps the load voltage at about $0.7\ \mathrm{V}$ (never negative), removes the negative excursion, and the average returns to the $13.5\ \mathrm{V}$ of the resistive formula, with the SCR turning off cleanly at $\pi$.
problems.ans: $V_{o,avg}=+13.5\ \mathrm{V}$ with a free-wheeling diode (the SCR turns off at $180^\circ$); with continuous inductor current and no free-wheeling path the extinction angle is $\beta=\pi+\alpha$ and $V_{o,avg}=V_m\cos\alpha/\pi=-27.0\ \mathrm{V}$ (inversion).
problems.trap: Applying the $\frac{V_m}{2\pi}(1+\cos\alpha)$ formula to an inductive load without checking the extinction angle. With large $L$ and no free-wheeling diode the current persists to $\beta=\pi+\alpha$, so at $\alpha=120^\circ$ the true average is $V_m\cos\alpha/\pi=-27.0\ \mathrm{V}$, not $+13.5\ \mathrm{V}$ — the sign itself is wrong.

problems.prompt: A single-phase half-wave controlled rectifier must deliver $V_{o,avg}=60\ \mathrm{V}$ to a resistive load from a $230\ \mathrm{V}$ rms, 50 Hz supply. Find the required firing angle and the extinction angle if the load becomes inductive and the current stays continuous.
steps: Uncontrolled half-wave average would be $V_m/\pi=103.5\ \mathrm{V}$, so $60\ \mathrm{V}$ needs delay.
$\alpha=\arccos(0.159)=80.9^\circ$, a late firing that leaves about 99 degrees of conduction.

For a resistive load the conduction ends at $180^\circ$; with an inductive load and no free-wheeling diode the extinction angle extends beyond $180^\circ$ and the average drops below $60\ \mathrm{V}$, so re-trigger earlier or add the free-wheeling diode.
problems.ans: $\alpha\approx80.9^\circ$; extinction stays at $180^\circ$ for a resistive load but moves past it for an inductive one, which lowers the delivered average.
problems.trap: Solving for $\alpha$ in radians and reporting $1.41$ instead of $80.9^\circ$, or forgetting to double-check the answer against the uncontrolled value $V_m/\pi=103.5\ \mathrm{V}$ — a firing angle of $80.9^\circ$ should give roughly 58 percent of full output, and $60/103.5=0.58$ confirms it.

traps: **Using the average voltage to find the load power.** At $\alpha=60^\circ$ a $50\ \Omega$ load from $120\ \mathrm{V}$ rms has $V_{avg}=40.5\ \mathrm{V}$ and $V_{rms}=107.6\ \mathrm{V}$; the power is $232\ \mathrm{W}$, not $V_{avg}I_{avg}=32.8\ \mathrm{W}$ — a factor of seven.
**Halving the bridge formula.** $V_{o,avg}=\frac{V_m}{\pi}(1+\cos\alpha)$ is the *bridge*; a single SCR uses the $2\pi$ denominator. Mixing them gives exactly a factor-of-two error in every problem.

**Ignoring the extinction angle with an RL load.** Above $\alpha=90^\circ$ an RL load without a free-wheeling diode drives $V_{o,avg}$ toward and past zero (inversion), so the resistive formula overstates the output by a large margin: at $\alpha=120^\circ$ with $V_m=169.7\ \mathrm{V}$ the resistive formula gives $+13.5\ \mathrm{V}$ while the fully smoothed current gives $V_m\cos\alpha/\pi=-27.0\ \mathrm{V}$ — the sign is wrong, not just the magnitude.

**Converting $\alpha$ for the $\sin2\alpha$ term incorrectly.** The RMS formulas need radians inside $\sin2\alpha$: $\alpha=60^\circ$ is $1.0472$ rad and $\sin120^\circ=0.866$, but typing $\sin(2\times60)=0.745$ (degrees-mode calculator) gives $V_{rms}=104.6\ \mathrm{V}$ instead of $107.6\ \mathrm{V}$.

**Forgetting that a narrow gate pulse may not latch.** The anode current must exceed the latching current $I_L$ before the pulse ends; a $1\ \mu\mathrm{s}$ spike driving a highly inductive load can fail to fire the SCR and produce a random half-cycle dropout, so use a wide pulse or a pulse train.

**Assuming the SCR turns off when the gate signal stops.** An SCR has no gate turn-off: once anode current exceeds the holding current $I_H$, removing the gate does nothing, and with continuous inductive current the device only stops at natural commutation or when the current is interrupted.
